facts.title: The Last Missing Element
facts.text: Promethium was the final naturally occurring element in the first seven rows of the periodic table to be discovered, leaving a stubborn gap at atomic number 61 for decades. Chemists in the 1920s and 1930s announced finds they called 'illinium' and 'florentium', but none could be confirmed. The genuine discovery only came in 1945, made by Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin, and Charles Coryell at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

facts.title: Born From Atom-Bomb Research
facts.text: Promethium was first isolated not from a mine but from the fission products of uranium inside a nuclear reactor during the Manhattan Project era. The team separated element 61 using ion-exchange chromatography, a then-new technique that could tease apart chemically similar rare-earth elements. Because of wartime secrecy, the discovery was not publicly announced until 1947.

facts.title: Named for a Fire-Stealing Titan
facts.text: The element is named after Prometheus, the Titan of Greek myth who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity. The name was suggested by Grace Mary Coryell, wife of team leader Charles Coryell, to symbolize both the daring of harnessing nuclear energy and a warning about its dangers. It is one of only a handful of elements named from Greek mythology.

facts.title: No Stable Form Exists
facts.text: Promethium is the only lanthanide and one of just two elements in the first 83 (the other being technetium) that has no stable isotopes whatsoever. Every one of its isotopes is radioactive and decays over time. This is a consequence of subtle nuclear physics: the nearby isotopes of neodymium and samarium are more energetically favorable, leaving promethium nowhere stable to sit.

facts.title: Vanishingly Rare on Earth
facts.text: Promethium does occur naturally, but in almost unimaginably tiny amounts produced by the spontaneous fission of uranium and the decay of europium in ores. Estimates suggest the entire Earth's crust contains only on the order of a few hundred grams of promethium at any moment. For practical purposes, all the promethium people use is manufactured artificially in reactors.

facts.title: It Glows in the Dark
facts.text: Promethium-147, with a half-life of about 2.6 years, emits low-energy beta particles that can make phosphors glow. It was once used in luminous paint for watch dials and instrument markings, replacing the far more dangerous radium. Because its beta radiation is weak and produces little penetrating gamma, it was considered a safer self-powered light source.

facts.title: A Battery That Lasts for Years
facts.text: Engineers built tiny 'nuclear batteries' (betavoltaic cells) using promethium-147, converting its steady beta decay into a trickle of electricity. These devices powered pacemakers, guided missiles, and space instruments where recharging was impossible. They could run for several years on a single source, limited mainly by the isotope's radioactive decay rather than by being used up like a chemical battery.

facts.title: Gauging Thickness Without Touching
facts.text: Industry uses promethium-147 sources in thickness gauges that measure materials like paper, plastic film, and sheet metal as they move along a production line. The beta particles pass through the material, and a detector reads how many get through, revealing the thickness instantly and without contact. This lets factories maintain precise, uniform output at high speed.

facts.title: The 2024 Solution Breakthrough
facts.text: For nearly 80 years, promethium's chemistry in water was poorly understood because so little of it could be handled safely. In 2024, scientists at Oak Ridge National Laboratory used X-ray spectroscopy to directly observe a promethium complex in solution for the first time. They measured its precise bond length to surrounding water and ligand atoms, finally pinning down a long-missing piece of rare-earth chemistry.

facts.title: Pinkish Salts and Shrinking Atoms
facts.text: Promethium compounds and solutions often show a pale pink or pinkish-yellow color, a result of how its electrons absorb visible light. The element fits neatly into the 'lanthanide contraction', the steady shrinking of atomic size across the rare-earth series as the nuclear charge pulls electrons inward. This contraction is why promethium and its neighbors behave so similarly and were historically so hard to separate.
